question: What is the main job of the epiglottis when you swallow food?

options.A: To produce sound through the vocal cords
options.B: To filter dust particles out of the nose
options.C: To warm and humidify incoming air
options.D: To cover the windpipe and prevent food from entering the lungs

explanation: Think of the epiglottis as a tiny trapdoor. When you swallow, it folds down over your windpipe so your food and drink safely slide down the esophagus instead of going into your lungs!

question: Which body part connects the back of the nose and mouth to the voice box (larynx)?
explanation: The pharynx is simply the muscular tube right behind your mouth and nasal cavity that acts as a highway, guiding air down toward your larynx and lungs.

question: What is the immediate danger when a person's upper airway gets blocked?

options.A: High blood pressure all over the body
options.B: Too much lung fluid being made
options.C: Blocked airflow leading to low oxygen (hypoxia)
options.D: The tiny air sacs in the lower lungs get too big

explanation: When the upper airway is blocked, fresh air can't get through to the lungs. This causes oxygen levels in the blood to drop fast—a condition we call hypoxia.

question: Why does a narrow upper airway cause a whistling or high-pitched breathing sound known as stridor?

options.A: The heart valves are clicking against the chest wall
options.B: Blood is rushing too fast through the neck veins
options.C: Mucus is vibrating inside the lower lung tissue
options.D: Air is forced rapidly through a tight, narrowed space

explanation: Stridor sounds a bit like wind whistling through a crack in a door. It happens when air has to squeeze forcefully through a narrowed airway passage.

question: Which of these conditions can cause sudden swelling of the soft tissues in the upper airway?
explanation: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction. It can cause rapid swelling in the face, tongue, and throat, which can dangerously close off the upper airway in minutes.

question: What is the most common reason an unconscious adult lying flat on their back stops breathing well?

options.A: The tiny air sacs in the lungs collapse
options.B: Their tongue falls backward and blocks the throat
options.C: Thick mucus builds up in the windpipe
options.D: The bronchial tubes go into a sudden spasm

explanation: When someone passes out, their muscles relax completely. Gravity takes over, causing the lower jaw and tongue to slump backward and block the pharynx.

question: Which breathing sound tells you right away that a patient has an upper airway obstruction?
explanation: Stridor is that high-pitched, strained sound you hear when air is struggling to push past a blockage in the upper airway. You can often hear it without a stethoscope!

question: A patient clutches their throat, cannot speak, and has blue lips. What is the best conclusion?

options.A: The patient is having a bad asthma flare-up.
options.B: Fluid is building up inside the lung air sacs.
options.C: The patient has a complete upper airway obstruction.
options.D: The patient is having a mild panic attack.

explanation: Clutching the throat is the universal sign of choking. Combined with not being able to speak and turning blue (cyanosis), it means air isn't getting through at all.

question: Why should you NOT send a patient with a blocked airway for a CT scan right away?

options.A: X-rays cannot show foreign objects at all.
options.B: The scanner is usually too far from the ward.
options.C: Contrast dye makes the vocal cords snap shut.
options.D: Keeping the airway open is always the top emergency priority.

explanation: An unstable airway can close up completely at any second. Saving the patient's life by securing their breathing always comes before moving them for pictures.

question: What is the very first quick check a nurse should do during an emergency airway assessment?

options.A: Listen for tummy sounds in all four quadrants
options.B: Look, listen, and feel for air movement
options.C: Check arterial blood gas lab results
options.D: Measure the exact size of the patient's neck

explanation: Keep it simple and fast! By looking at the chest, listening near the mouth, and feeling for breath, you instantly know if air is moving in and out.

question: How do abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver) help a choking person?

options.A: They drain trapped fluid from the lower lungs
options.B: They force trapped air upward to pop the object out
options.C: They help the heart pump blood faster
options.D: They help the patient relax their vocal cords

explanation: Abdominal thrusts squeeze the diaphragm upward. This creates a quick puff of artificial air from the lungs that acts like a cough to push the blockage out.

question: A choking patient suddenly passes out and falls to the floor. What should you do right away?

options.A: Start chest compressions and check the mouth for the object
options.B: Prepare to perform a surgical opening in the neck
options.C: Give an emergency injection of adrenaline
options.D: Prop the patient up in a high sitting position in bed

explanation: Once a choking victim collapses, you transition into CPR. Pumping the chest helps push air against the blockage, and you can check the mouth to scoop out the object if you see it.

question: What is the emergency procedure where a tiny cut is made in the neck membrane to open a blocked airway?
explanation: A cricothyroidotomy is an emergency lifesaving move. When nothing else works and the upper airway is fully shut, healthcare providers cut through the cricothyroid membrane to create a direct path for air.

question: Why would a doctor choose a tracheostomy instead of keeping a breathing tube through the mouth long-term?

options.A: It completely stops any risk of getting an infection
options.B: It means you never have to clean around the site or use suction
options.C: It is much more comfortable and safer for long-term breathing support
options.D: It is much faster to do in an outdoor emergency

explanation: Having a tube taped through the mouth for weeks can damage the vocal cords and mouth. A tracheostomy provides a secure, comfortable airway right through the neck for patients who need long-term help.

question: What vital equipment must always be kept ready at the bedside of a patient recovering from an airway issue?

options.A: A standard blood pressure cuff and stethoscope
options.B: Suction machine and a manual breathing bag
options.C: A sterile surgical tray for major tummy surgery
options.D: An intravenous infusion pump with extra tubing

explanation: Always be prepared! Having suction and a bag-valve-mask right at the bedside lets nurses act instantly if thick mucus blocks the airway or breathing slows down.

question: What is the most helpful advice a nurse can give to a patient who frequently chokes on their food?

options.A: Take a strong sleeping pill before meals to relax
options.B: Cut food into small pieces and avoid talking while chewing
options.C: Drink a large glass of cold water with every bite
options.D: Lie flat on your back right after finishing your meal

explanation: Simple habits make a big difference. Taking small bites, chewing thoroughly, and focusing on your food instead of chatting helps prevent accidental choking.
